name: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate
lead: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate (SAP) is a water-soluble, phosphate-ester derivative of vitamin C used in skincare, mainly as an antioxidant. People use it in serums and creams to try to even skin tone, soften fine lines and calm breakouts, with the practical draw that it is promoted as more stable than L-ascorbic acid, which oxidises readily.[1][6] The Cosmetic Ingredient Review's safety assessment of ascorbic acid and its salts and esters, including SAP, describes them as functioning primarily as antioxidants in cosmetic formulations.[1]

Human trials include a randomised, double-blind acne study comparing 5% SAP, 0.2% retinol and the combination, a double-blind comparison of 5% SAP and 5% ascorbic acid emulgels on crow's feet wrinkles, and a split-face sebum study of a combined ascorbyl palmitate and SAP emulsion.[14][15][16] A 2026 systematic review of vitamin C in dermatology reports that SAP improves texture and pigmentation, particularly when paired with microneedling.[17]
Laboratory studies have examined SAP's stability in microemulsions and in formulations containing lipoic acid and vitamins A and E.[2][3]

chain: Phosphate ester is applied to skin as a stable vitamin C form
Skin enzymes are described as releasing active vitamin C, an antioxidant
Claimed: more even tone, fewer inflamed acne lesions and softer lines
angle.text: People apply SAP serums and creams to try to improve brightness, uneven pigmentation, acne marks and fine lines. Trials have tested 5% SAP products on acne lesions, wrinkles and oiliness.

paras: Vitamin C is described as labile, with oxidation accelerated by light, oxygen, heat and higher pH [6]. Derivatives such as SAP are used partly to address this. Studies have investigated SAP in microemulsions [2], liposomes for cutaneous photoprotection [7], and hyaluronic acid microspheres for dermal delivery [8].

SAP appears in water-based serums, lotions and emulgels, sometimes paired with other actives. Trials have used it alone and with retinol, and with ascorbyl palmitate (an oil-soluble ester) in a multiple emulsion to cover both water and oil phases of the skin.[14][16] Dermatology reviews group it with other derivatives such as ascorbyl glucoside and tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate, noting that ascorbic acid remains the most clinically validated form while derivatives are chosen for stability or tolerance.[17]

sections.h: Why vitamin C is used on skin
paras: Wikipedia describes vitamin C as a cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, a step that lets collagen form its triple helix, and as an antioxidant that scavenges reactive oxygen and nitrogen species; in scurvy, the defective collagen and skin spots are described as reversible with repletion.[6] These roles are the usual starting point for putting vitamin C derivatives such as SAP on the skin in the hope of firmer-looking, more even skin.[6]

The same article describes vitamin C as one of the most labile vitamins, with oxidation accelerated by light, oxygen, heat and higher pH, in its discussion of food; formulators cite the same fragility as the reason to use a phosphate ester like SAP in skincare.[6]
The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel's final safety assessment covered SAP together with ascorbic acid and several salts for use in cosmetics [1].

A comparison of vitamin C derivatives in topical formulations containing lipoic acid, vitamin A and vitamin E examined their stability [3]. Related work on ascorbyl palmitate in microemulsions studied stability of that derivative [9].

SAP has also been used in non-cosmetic experiments, including a hydrogel with stem cells for wound healing in mice and diabetic rats [10][11] and in studies of restoring bond strength after tooth bleaching [12]. Reviews and experiments have also tested SAP's effect on osteoblasts and its use as an antioxidant in packaging films.[18][19]

A randomised, double-blind trial compared 5% SAP, 0.2% retinol and the two together in acne. SAP reduced inflammatory lesions by 20.14 percent at 4 weeks and 48.82 percent at 8 weeks, retinol by 21.79 and 49.50 percent, and the combination by 29.28 and 63.10 percent.[14]

A blinded, placebo-controlled study of emulgels containing 5% SAP or 5% ascorbic acid on the crow's feet area of healthy volunteers found both reduced wrinkle depth and improved elasticity, with no statistically significant difference between them; the authors note that stabilising agents are needed for both preparations.[15] An 11-volunteer, 90-day split-face study of a combined ascorbyl palmitate and SAP multiple emulsion reported reduced facial sebum secretion against control.[16]

A completed trial registered as NCT00714454 tested a 5% sodium L-ascorbyl-2-phosphate lotion for acne vulgaris.[4] A registered trial (NCT04835259, status unknown, n=90) examined topical antioxidants for photoaging,[5] and a 300-person phase 3 trial studied an antioxidant dentifrice for gingivitis.[13]

card.summary: A stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative; formulation data are plentiful, human appearance outcomes are sparse.
card.note: Registered acne and photoaging trials exist but outcomes were not located.

quick.overview:
Sodium ascorbyl phosphate is a stabilised, water-soluble form of vitamin C used as a cosmetic antioxidant.
Most published work covers formulation and stability; human trials of its looks effects are few.
quick.mechanism: It functions primarily as an antioxidant in cosmetic formulations, per the Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment.
quick.risks: A cosmetic safety assessment covers SAP alongside other vitamin C compounds; no specific harms were identified.
